items.body: There is a useful contradiction at the centre of “Fame Fatale”: NER\OGRIS have become more precise about their identity at exactly the moment they seem most interested in introducing instability into it. KaiN talks about preserving sounds that drift, distort or sit slightly outside the grid; TinoC writes about people attempting to maintain individuality inside systems that make behaviour increasingly predictable. In both cases, the problem is similar: what happens when something becomes so optimised, visible or controllable that it begins to lose the qualities that made it individual in the first place? That makes “Fame Fatale” a considerably more interesting second album than a simple refinement of “I Am the Shadow, I Am the Light”. Its production can be meticulous without aspiring to cleanliness; analogue instability is deliberately left inside digital construction, and influences from industrial electronics and highly polished pop production are allowed to coexist without being reconciled into one obvious aesthetic. KaiN’s distinction between nostalgia and influence is particularly revealing: rather than reproducing an earlier decade, he wants to extract physical qualities from it, warmth, hiss, instability, and place them against sounds that belong unmistakably to the present. TinoC approaches the present from another direction. He still rejects the role of commentator with a programme or mission, describing the lyrics as observations of what happens around him. Yet those observations now repeatedly encounter social-media visibility, manipulated information and the increasingly strange relationship between individuality and mass behaviour. Even the sarcastic mutation of femme fatale into “Fame Fatale” turns attention itself into part of the problem. I spoke with TinoC and KaiN about why technical mistakes can become the most valuable part of a recording, the difference between influence and reconstruction, digital perfection and analogue resistance, social-media fame, the uncomfortable politics of attention, and why NER\OGRIS may eventually move in a much quieter direction than “Fame Fatale” suggests. FAME FATALE by ner.ogris Karo: When we spoke in 2023, Kai described NER\OGRIS as perhaps the more “grown-up” continuation of ideas that had existed elsewhere, while “I Am the Shadow, I Am the Light” still felt like a project discovering its own internal logic. Three years later, “Fame Fatale” sounds much more certain about what belongs inside NER\OGRIS and what does not. Do you now feel that the project has acquired a language of its own, or is recognising that language precisely the point at which you become suspicious of it and start trying to break it? TinoC: For me, N\OG has its own, maybe unique style. And I think this matters, because otherwise all my other bands and projects wouldn’t make sense. But we are talking about N\OG, so when we compare the beginning of 2022, when the band started, with now, or rather with the point when the album developed, we were in a completely different situation. When we assembled IATS-IATL, we had several tracks and had to find a selection for the album. For some of those tracks, I wrote lyrics. That is, in short, the story of the first album. For “Fame Fatale”, we had to start from scratch. It means the cat was out of the bag: the band was there, the music was there, and some people had and have expectations. I honestly hope that we managed to create music which people will recognise as N\OG, but also recognise that there is progress, change or new facets. Karo: The phrase “Fame Fatale” is immediately suggestive because fame traditionally implies being seen, while the album seems preoccupied with a world in which visibility no longer guarantees understanding; everything is exposed, circulated and measured, yet what matters becomes harder to locate. What does “fame” mean in the title? Are you talking literally about celebrity, or about a broader condition in which ordinary people are increasingly required to perform themselves for attention? TinoC: The name of the album is a little ironic, or has a decent dose of sarcasm in it. Most of the tracks, lyrically, are about people and their issues trying to “survive” their daily lives. And yes, the so-called “fame” they gain from social media is in fact fatal. I don’t remember exactly why we decided to edit the French phrase femme fatale into the album name, but I am sure there was a reason. 😉 Karo: In our previous conversation, Tino, you said something I found quite important: “I am not on a mission. I am just a guy who writes about some topics at one point of his life.” “Fame Fatale”, however, moves through manipulation, social tension, distorted truth, isolation and attention becoming a currency. Has the scale of what provokes you changed? Are these still fundamentally personal observations, or has it become impossible to write about private anxiety without also writing about the systems producing it? TinoC: I am still this guy who writes about things I see and hear, and topics that move me in some way. I haven’t written an autobiographical or biographical song for a very long time, so to answer the question: they are still observations, because there is A LOT of shit going on at the moment. Karo: The album’s central idea seems to involve a strange paradox: we have unprecedented access to information and unprecedented difficulty deciding what deserves our trust or attention. Music itself now exists inside exactly that economy, competing with infinite content, algorithms and increasingly abbreviated forms of listening. Did making an album about fractured attention affect the way you thought about the album format itself? Is asking somebody to stay inside a complete NER\OGRIS record now almost a countercultural demand? TinoC: Fun fact: you nailed it in some way. As you said, all the information is there, the knowledge is there, but people decide to believe in a damn AI clip in their timeline. In the end, the album is about the fact that almost the entire mankind is fucked. A lot of people are telling this to the people who are obviously more fucked than others, and the result is that the more fucked people decide to declare that they are the elite now. In this case, I am guilty too: I make music because I want to be heard. 😉 Karo: The musical coordinates around “Fame Fatale” are unusually broad. Skinny Puppy and Front Line Assembly represent abrasion, experimentation and industrial pressure, while Trevor Horn and Frankie Goes To Hollywood represent almost obsessive studio construction, scale and pop precision. Those are not obvious neighbours. Is the interesting territory for NER\OGRIS now found exactly between those approaches: allowing something to remain ugly, unstable or threatening while producing it with enormous attention to beauty and detail? TinoC: Let’s suppose we knew what we were doing and could control the direction we were heading… I think we’d try exactly what you’re describing. 😉 KaiN: Yes, exactly there, and I think the analogue/digital tension is part of why that space works. Everything today is made inside a computer. Everything can be perfectly in time, perfectly in tune, and that’s precisely what makes it sound so replaceable. So while we build things with a lot of digital precision, I try to smuggle in something that resists it: a hardware synth that drifts slightly, a distorted signal, a take that isn’t fixed to the grid. That friction between ugly or unstable and beautiful or precise is basically the friction between analogue and digital. In this very digital time, I want that friction, that dirt, to stay audible. It’s good for the ears, even when it hurts a little. Karo: “Fame Fatale” clearly draws on electronic music with a long history behind it, yet it never feels interested in reconstructing a particular decade. How do you distinguish between influence and nostalgia when you work? Is there a point where knowing the history of a sound becomes useful precisely because it allows you to detach it from its original context and make it mean something different now? TinoC: I mean, if I were a musician, maybe I could monitor or manage my work. Because I am not, I follow my instincts, or the music just happens. And this happens in a way I like, which I feel, and turns into music I personally like. And yes, I love two decades in music history. That’s why almost everything I do is an homage to that sound, or maybe I simply can’t do it differently. KaiN: For me the difference is this: nostalgia wants to recreate a decade; influence wants to steal one physical quality from it and drag it into now. I don’t want to make a record that sounds like it was made in the ’80s or ’90s. I want the warmth, the hiss, the slight instability that analogue gear from those eras had, and then put that texture next to something that is completely of today. That’s less about a specific decade and more about not wanting music to sound too clean. Karo: Kai, when we spoke before, you described moments when a single sound could trigger an entire composition, sometimes producing things you later could not quite reconstruct yourself. With “Fame Fatale”, has increased control made those accidental moments harder to preserve? How do you stop a highly developed production process from correcting the very accidents that gave a track its personality? KaiN: Control and accident aren’t really opposites for me; they’re two different phases of the same process. That moment where one sound triggers a whole track almost never happens once the setup is “finished”. It happens early, when I don’t quite know what I’m doing yet: a filter set wrong, a random modulation routing, a preset I only meant to check for two seconds. The further a track moves into production, the bigger the temptation to smooth exactly those “mistakes” out, because technically they’re not clean. With “Fame Fatale”, I tried to slow that down on purpose, bouncing the raw early version quickly and then building around it instead of endlessly “fixing” the original sound. Sometimes that means something in the final track is technically wrong. But that’s usually its personality. So I use control to protect the accident rather than to correct it. Karo: Musically, “Fame Fatale” seems interested in two apparently contradictory ideas: abrasion and scale on one side, meticulous construction and memorable melody on the other. How do you decide when a sound should remain harsh, unstable or even ugly, and when it needs to become beautiful? Can excessive refinement actually weaken the emotional truth of a track? KaiN: For me, it’s less a rule and more a question I ask about every sound: what is it doing emotionally in that moment? If a harsh, unstable element is carrying the tension or the threat in a track, smoothing it out doesn’t make the song better; it just makes it quieter emotionally. A bit of analogue dirt, something slightly off, slightly warm, slightly wrong, does something to your ear that perfection can’t. So my test isn’t “does this sound good?” It’s “does this still feel true?” If the answer is no, I go back. Karo: The debut used contrast almost as an organising principle: shadow and light, ambient passages against harder electronics, even the distinction between Spanish instrumental titles and English vocal pieces. “Fame Fatale” still works through opposition, but the contrasts seem less clean now; vulnerability can exist inside aggression, seduction inside something deeply uncomfortable, and highly controlled electronic structures can carry a sense of instability. Has your understanding of contrast changed from placing opposites beside one another to allowing them to occupy the same moment? TinoC: Obviously we have fewer instrumental tracks on the album, and you are right, the tracks are a bit faster or straighter. The exception is “Graves”, which for me is a genius weirdo. 😉 Karo: “A View” is the first piece from “Fame Fatale” that we encounter together with a visual narrative, and I found the message of the video strikingly pessimistic. There seems to be very little faith in our ability to distinguish observation from manipulation, or simply to step outside the systems shaping what we see. What was the original concept behind the video, and how closely does your own interpretation correspond to that rather bleak reading? TinoC: The video itself is a medium to transport the lyrics. The lyrics are maybe the second optimistic words I have ever written, but the protagonist struggles. He, she or it struggles a lot and mourns about it in a very sad way. It’s not the point that he, she or it feels betrayed or manipulated, just fucked by everything. Karo: You are taking “Fame Fatale” on the road in autumn, moving through Prague, Germany, Sweden, France and Belgium. You previously told me that NER\OGRIS live is deliberately not a reproduction of the record; the backing tracks are rebuilt for performance, synths and effects are manipulated live, and there is room for controlled chaos. Has that philosophy changed as the music has become more detailed and cinematic? At what point does preserving the architecture of a production begin to compete with the danger that makes a live electronic show exciting? TinoC: Kai adds some sounds and noises to the tracks and T uses his voice, so “controlled chaos” is maybe a big word for what we will do on the tour, but there will be some differences from the album versions. KaiN: It’s true that we’re not trying to reproduce the record one-to-one, and for me that’s partly a control question again. A purely digital backing track never changes, never breaks, never surprises anyone, including us. So live, some of what I add is deliberately analogue or hardware-based, things that can drift a little from night to night. It’s a small risk, but it keeps the show honest, and it’s very much in line with how I feel about the whole album: in a time where everything can sound perfect, a bit of unpredictability, a bit of dirt, is what actually makes it feel alive. Karo: “Fame Fatale” arrives only three years after your debut and one year after “Silenci”, so NER\OGRIS still feels like a project moving unusually quickly rather than settling into a comfortable cycle. Looking beyond this album and the upcoming tour, what part of NER\OGRIS still feels unexplored to each of you? Is there something you have already discovered about the project that you deliberately have not used yet because the right record, collaboration or context for it has not arrived? TinoC: As always, I personally think that “my” best song has not been written yet. Let’s see if I am wrong or right. KaiN: There are ideas we’ve already found and deliberately not used, sounds or directions that felt too far away from what “Fame Fatale” needed to be. I think there’s still a much quieter, more minimal side of NER\OGRIS that we haven’t shown yet, almost the opposite of the scale and abrasion on this record. Whether that becomes its own release or just one track on the next album, I don’t know yet. But it’s sitting there, waiting for the right context, not the right idea. About NER\OGRIS NER\OGRIS is the German electronic duo of Kai Neugebauer and Tino Claus. Neugebauer is the founder of Les Berrtas and works on the musical and production side of NER\OGRIS, while Claus is known as the vocalist of Amnistia and through projects including TC75 and MRDTC. The two first met in 2014; the project itself formed in February 2022. Its name combines nero, Italian for black, with gris, French and Spanish for grey. The collaboration began when Neugebauer had been preparing instrumental material and Claus heard one of the pieces and immediately imagined vocals for it. What began as an experiment developed into NER\OGRIS and their debut album, “I Am the Shadow – I Am the Light”, released in February 2023 through Dependent Records; Side-Line reported the first single in Ner\Ogris release first video single ‘Deepest Fear’ taken from forthcoming debut album ‘I Am The Shadow – I Am The Light’ and spoke to the duo in the Click Interview with Ner\Ogris: ‘A Strong Name That Reflects Our Philosophy’. The album established many of the contrasts that remained central to the project: analogue and digital sound, ambient space and rhythmic pressure, melody and dissonance. The six-track mini-album “Silenci” followed on 1 November 2025. Its production credits already established the division of labour behind the duo: music and production by KaiN, words and vocals by TinoC, with mastering by Arnte of Pyrroline. “Fame Fatale” is the duo’s second full-length album and is scheduled for 2 October 2026, with the pre-sale and the autumn dates reported here in NER\OGRIS launch ‘Fame Fatale’ pre-sale, confirm tour with Fïx8:Sëd8. Its nine tracks are “Calls”, “Antithese”, “Lack of Proof”, “A View”, “Graves”, “La Hora El Ganador”, “Glowing in the Dark”, “Unter Menschen” and “Dulcimer”. NER\OGRIS will take the album on the road in autumn, beginning at Prague’s Futurum Music Bar on 17 October. Their current official listings continue through Münster, Stockholm, Gothenburg, Lille, Liège, Hannover, Freiberg, Berlin and Schmalkalden, with the final currently announced date on 28 November 2026.

items.body: Cedric Wattergniaux has been active under the alias Kilmarth for several years now. With “Au Bord Des Ténèbres”, he returns with his third album, self-released this time and also available as a limited-edition vinyl release. The eight tracks draw inspiration from artist Pierre Soulages’ concept of ‘Outrenoir’. Kilmarth adapts this concept to the human experience, exploring the idea that black is never the final destination. Naturally, the music is the main focus here, and in this regard, Wattergniaux seems—for the first time—to have found a truly consistent musical direction. Gone are the guest vocalists, Jazzy influences, and Latin American experiments. Instead, the entire album is built around Experimental-Electro, Glitch, and occasional Cinematic influences. Some might not consider this the most accessible music, yet Kilmarth surprises the listener with cold soundscapes that are sometimes underpinned by a melodic touch, but are primarily defined by an overwhelming array of sound manipulations and effects, creating a truly grim atmosphere. Occasional spoken-word samples add genuine value to the mix. Another significant improvement can be heard in the mixing and overall production, areas in which Kilmarth has made great strides. In short, this album was a pleasant surprise. It demonstrates real potential and paves the way for even greater things to come. Kilmarth seems ready to take the next step and is sure to appeal to fans of labels such as Ant-Zen. (Rating:8). The album was preceded by the three-track single “Avant de céder…”, covered in Kilmarth releases three-track single ‘Avant de céder…’ as prelude to upcoming album, and Wattergniaux discussed the Soulages concept behind the record in Kilmarth interview: the light inside Pierre Soulages’ black on ‘Au bord des Ténèbres…’. Listen to “Outrenoir”: Outrenoir by Kilmarth About Kilmarth Kilmarth is the solo project of Belgian musician Cedric Wattergniaux, working in IDM, glitch and post-industrial ambient. Side-Line first covered the project in 2018 with the ‘Click Interview’ with Kilmarth: ‘Music Is A Legal Drug That Has The Immense Power To Make Us Escape’, published on 19 August 2018, and reviewed the CD mini-album “Catharsis” the same year. The EP Kilmarth – Derrière Le Miroir (EP – Kilmarth) followed in 2021, together with a video for “M-Fia41”. The two-track single “Baryum” arrived in January 2022 and the mini-album Kilmarth – Better Days (EP – Kilmarth) in 2023, the first Kilmarth release with a guest singer. The debut full-length Kilmarth – Sociological Veranda (Album – Kilmarth) was released in January 2024, preceded by the glitch single “Vergessen”, and the IDM EP “My Son of The Moon” followed in November 2024. In January 2025 Wattergniaux teamed up with D-Fried for the album “Micrometeoritic Flowerpot”. The concept album Kilmarth – Cherophobia (Digital Album – Adventurous Music), built around the fear of happiness, was issued in January 2026 through the Adventurous Music digital series. “Au Bord Des Ténèbres…” was released on 6 June 2026 on Bandcamp and holds eight tracks, opening with “Le seuil” and closing with “Outrenoir”. It is the first Kilmarth album pressed on vinyl.

items.body: You’ll be food for a hawk if you live like a lamb the hours decay like a corpse in the sand eternity calls and we’re singing for the damned There are records that announce their mortality with violins and candlelight, and then there are records that sound as if somebody has kicked open the crypt door. 1919’s Last Dance of the Departed, their first studio release since 2021 and first 7” since 1983, belongs to the latter breed: hard bass, serrated guitar, drums with the discipline of factory machinery, and Rio Goldhammer singing as though the end of civilization has inconvenienced him personally. 1919’s Bradford roots place them among the original wave of groups that pushed post-punk into darker territory during the early 1980s. Bands like Bauhaus and the Virgin Prunes were contemporaries in establishing what would later be called “goth”, working in parallel from different cities with a related vocabulary of skeletal guitars, theatrical dread, physical rhythm, and damaged religious imagery. On Last Dance of the Departed, 1919 carries that vocabulary forward with the blunt force of musicians who have spent years dragging these songs through clubs rather than preserving them behind glass. Ding Archer’s bass gives the track a heavy, stalking center, the guitar cuts across it in cold diagonal strokes, and the drums maintain a martial insistence that makes mortality feel strangely danceable. Last Dance of the Departed stares directly at extinction: brother killing brother, wages exchanged for useless possessions, gods who may have stopped answering the telephone, and the ridiculous persistence of hope. Goldhammer delivers these ideas with enough bite to prevent the song from collapsing into gothic sermonizing. There is black humour buried in the fatalism, the sort that develops when you have been around long enough to know death is coming so you may as well crank up the amp to give him a proper fanfare. The production leaves plenty of exposed bone. Guitar, bass, and percussion occupy their own hostile corners, colliding without becoming muddy, while Goldhammer rides above the racket with a voice closer to a public warning than a conventional rock performance. The video, directed by Goldhammer, pushes that idea into the flesh. Live footage flashes through a band still throwing itself at the stage after decades marked by departures and death. Members have been lost along the way, and the song carries that knowledge without converting grief into museum-piece reverence. These musicians still look dangerous because they remain committed to movement, volume, friction, and the communal absurdity of standing in a room together while the clock keeps chewing through time and space. Watch the video for Last Dance of the Departed below: For a band whose early history includes Cry Wolf, Machine, and two Peel sessions, 1919 sounds remarkably uninterested in reenacting 1983. Their post-punk remains angular and severe, but age has thickened the music’s sense of consequence. Last Dance of the Departed knows the party ends, knows the gods may be absent, knows the body goes back to ash, and still finds enough electricity in that knowledge to keep the dead dancing. 1919’s Last Dance of the Departed and its B-side Satellite Man are available on black and limited-edition green 7″ Vinyl. Order here. items.album: We Have A Commentary: “EBM Club Classics (Disc 1)”

items.body: Our monthly We Have A Commentary bonus podcast works a bit differently this month; with Alex being off in the UK we’ve prerecorded a double dose of discussion of Synthetic Symphony’s 1998 comp “EBM Club Classics”, with the first disc dropping today and the second this coming Sunday. Disc one functioned as a handy DJ tool in the late 90s and early 00s, linking some of the first cuts from the likes of And One, Leaether Strip, and Bigod 20 with contemporary state of the art from Covenant, while also throwing in some left-field choices and proto-EBM cuts which have us speculating about the genre and the idea of an EBM canon at large. Tune back in this Sunday for the second half! As always, you can rate and subscribe on iTunes, download directly, or listen through the widget down below. items.body: One of my hobbyhorses I love to beat—likely familiar to longtime readers—is that percussionists often make the most interesting composers: Steve Reich, Egisto Macchi, Iannis Xenakis, Edgar Varése, John Cage, Lou Harrison, Karlheinz Stockhausen, Art Blakey, Max Roach, Paul Motian, Jack DeJohnette, Milford Graves, Susie Ibarra, Valentina Magaletti… I could go on and on. Rhythm is one of the ways we structure time, and in this percussionists seem to think differently about the architecture of music in unique ways. Attack, resonance, and duration dominate their vocabulary, while pitch and harmony are often less centered. It was Steve Reich who first inspired this intuition in me, but I first articulated it as such when I learned that Sasu Ripatti (best known as Vladislav Delay) was trained as a drummer. As he explained to Fifteen Questions, I started at the age of 5 with classical percussion and drums, jazz later on, death metal in between. I switched from sticks to electronic equipment and music production at about the age of 20, in ’96, and released my first productions in ’97. The off-kilter rhythms of Vladislav Delay are rooted in part in jazz, and even the relatively dance friendly music of Luomo, Ripatti’s deep house project (see 2000’s beloved masterpiece Vocalcity), makes more sense in this light. But this influence seemed to be a formative one, the roots, rather than a window into Ripatti’s creative process. As Vladislav Delay, Ripatti is granted the freedom to pursue whatever, while Luomo operates within the form of a relatively codified dance music genre of microhouse. Ripatti has occasionally wheeled out other monikers to pursue other directions, for instance footwork and juke through his Ripatti series, and later happy hardcore as Ripatti Deluxe on his newly minted Rajaton imprint (see 2022’s Speed Demon). There’s something surprisingly captivating about much of this later, frenetic, high-tempo work, although in truth it often makes me feel much too anxious for the era we’ve been living in. But even when a particular record or style doesn’t land with me, it still reveals something about the artist that helps unlock aspects of his other records. Like the Blues, innovation isn’t occurring on the level of form but of expression. Having the contrast of the free form persona allows us to better hear the artist’s style manifest from the limited gestures available within the conventions of other genres. It was the release of Whistleblower (2007) that transformed me into a committed fan, with earlier records including Multila (2000), Anima (2001), and The Four Quarters (2005) becoming some of my favorite records of all time. But it was Tummaa (2009) that changed how I thought about Ripatti’s process. Ripatti and his partner AGF had left Berlin, relocating their family to a remote Finnish island in the Baltic Sea, where they still live, and Tummaa feels like a rebirth worthy of this change. That record features Lucio Capece on bass clarinet and soprano sax and Craig Armstrong on Rhodes piano, with Ripatti playing percussion and shaping the results as a producer and composer. For whatever reason, Tummaa seems to get lost in the (admittedly excellent and crowded) discography, but I’ve increasingly come to see it as a missing link between classic VD records and the ensembles he would later work with. Sasu Ripatti has been quietly releasing new VD and Luomo material since late last year, and in May 2026 released the surprisingly acoustic vd5 on Finland’s We Jazz label. In our spring preview earlier this year, Richard wrote that “Vladislav Delay is now a quintet.” In fact, we had heard a preview in 2020 in the form of a live video, but unless you were a subscriber (or there for the live show at Teatro do Bairro Alto in Lisbon), this probably went under the radar. That Bandcamp subscriber exclusive also noted that “there will be an album eventually with the group,” and that time has finally arrived. Fifteen years earlier, Vladislav Delay had already become the Vladislav Delay Quartet, consisting of Derek Shirley on acoustic bass, Lucio Capece on reeds and effects, Mika Vainio on electronics and live processing, and Delay on drums and percussion and postproduction. I love the physicality and ambiguous electroacoustic timbres of this record, and had hoped for more (perhaps even a live set at Mutek), but of course, the tragic death of Mika Vainio in 2017 put an end to that. And Vainio is impossible to replace, so expanding further into a quintet is a logical move. In addition to the returning Derek Shirley and Lucio Capece, Ripatti is joined by Maria Bertel on trombone, and frequent collaborator Max Loderbauer, who played Buchla on the 2020 recording and perhaps most surprisingly here contributes piano. Ripatti and Loderbauer rounded out the Moritz von Oswald Trio, who I vaguely recall seeing at Mutek in 2010(?), but I was much more blown away by a bill that included Delay, Tim Hecker, Ben Frost, and CM von Hausswolff. I mean, come on! I was discovering the Basic Channel and Rhythm and Sound catalogues at this point, but the Trio never resonated as deeply with me. Even if I rarely revisit the Trio records, I did appreciate seeing Ripatti in the context of a live band, playing acoustic instruments with analog effects, strongly signaling a gesturality that is harder to perceive in his electronic works. While those trio records never quite grabbed me, they clearly cemented Ripatti and Loderbauer’s rapport. Shortly after the release of the Quartet record, Ripatti and Loderbauer left von Oswald’s trio (they both appear on 2012’s Fetch), and the two would continue to work together as Heisenberg. Some years later, Ripatti emerged from a quiet period, contributing percussion and electronics to Nils Petter Molvær’s aptly titled Nordub (2018), which also involved Eivind Aarset on guitar and Sly & Robbie holding down the rhythm section. A very nice project, but a bit restrained, perhaps, clearly aimed for bourgeois audiences in refined theatres rather than dank basements and hazy bedrooms. The experience must have been a dream for Ripatti, however, who would later fly to Kingston to further collaborate with the reggae legends, sessions that resulted in 500-Push-Up (2020), distilling the group dynamic to raw rhythm section excursions. (Both Sly and Robbie, too, have sadly passed on in the years since.) Delay continues stubbornly chasing his own vision. Sasu Ripatti is never one to get too comfortable, preferring to take the more difficult road, reinventing himself time and again. Perhaps this is what has led him to so many collaborations. In addition to those ensembles previously mentioned, we should mention records with his partner Antye Greie as AGF / Delay and RyJ, Sensate Focus with Mark Fell, and most recently ZWAARD, with Antipop MC Beans. But as much as I love a good duo, there is something magical about an ensemble. On vd5, Ripatti trades the brittle and dystopian electronics of the late Mika Vainio for the warm, impressionistic touch of Max Loderbauer’s piano and Maria Bertel’s trombone, playing off Capece’s woodwinds and Derek Shirley’s bass. Recorded at Berlin’s Candybomber by Ingo Krauss, mixed by Ripatti himself, and mastered by Juho Luukkainen, the album marks a fundamental shift in the group’s center of gravity. Where the Quartet record felt like a clenched mechanical fist—a thicket of vibrating reeds, deep bass, and corroded signal—the Quintet opens into a more porous breathing space. The Quartet was slow, abrasive, and texturally heavy; the 2020 live take on this material trafficked in similar drone textures and feedback while searching for their own identity. But vd5 is a different animal. At forty-five minutes, the ten tracks are simply titled with numbers—though not in sequence. The album opens with “two” before moving to “twelve” and “nineteen,” while the closing track is, fittingly, “three,” hinting at a larger suite from which these pieces were selected. Despite this fragmented taxonomy, vd5 is unmistakably a Delay record; the space still feels meticulously sculpted, the silence carefully hewn, but the palette is overwhelmingly acoustic and warmly resonant. This is a mature, generous iteration of his vision, and arguably his most immediately rewarding ensemble work since Vainio’s passing. The album unfurls slowly. Opener “two” establishes the core tensions: Loderbauer’s piano offers harmonic anchor rather than abstraction, while the acoustic sighs from Capece’s sax and Shirley’s bass are met with Bertel’s molten trombone. Ripatti’s own kit work is characteristically fractured, ghosting around the pulse rather than driving it, less of a timekeeper and more of a textural instigator. Elsewhere, “nine” foregrounds horn harmonies and deep bass, ranking among the darkest cuts on the record. Midway through, the group locks into a loping, almost meditative groove on “thirteen” that recalls not the dub-like spacing of Tummaa but an acoustic version of the 2010s VD records for Raster-Noton, with their uneven kick patterns and warbling melodies. “Fifteen” comes closest to the plodding dissonance of the Quartet, making it the most foreboding and insistent track here, yet strangely also one of the most “jazz”-sounding, beginning in gloom before resolving into something almost uplifting. Closer “three” picks up where the opener left off, dissolving into sustained, sinister drones, the musicians’ breath overwhelmed by noise. Is it “jazz”? Who cares. Ripatti isn’t just programming rhythms; he’s composing with attack, resonance, and silence through a living ensemble. And it’s the largely acoustic, real-time interplay of that ensemble that elevates vd5, making it a must-hear record for fans of Vladislav Delay. If rhythm is how we structure time, then vd5 finds Ripatti carving out a temporality that feels less like a loop and more like a tide; it’s a testament to a lifelong percussionist’s ear for the life that exists strictly between the beats. (Joseph Sannicandro)

items.excerpt: BALTHVS take the title of “Pale Blue Dot” from Carl Sagan, who used the phrase for the Earth as Voyager 1 photographed it in 1990: a single point of light six billion kilometres from the lens. The Bogotá trio are declared Sagan fans, and they turn his warning into one blunt question: “Why destroy the one place that we call home, while there is nowhere else to go anyway?” The single announces MANIFEST, the band’s sixth album, out on Mixto Records on 7 October. items.body: BALTHVS take the title of “Pale Blue Dot” from Carl Sagan, who used the phrase for the Earth as Voyager 1 photographed it in 1990: a single point of light six billion kilometres from the lens. The Bogotá trio are declared Sagan fans, and they turn his warning into one blunt question: “Why destroy the one place that we call home, while there is nowhere else to go anyway?” The single announces MANIFEST, the band’s sixth album, out on Mixto Records on 7 October. Guitarist Balthazar Aguirre leads the trio with drummer Santiago Lizcano and bassist Johanna Mercuriana, who returns for this album after stepping away from touring to raise a child. The three regrouped in the Colombian countryside and wrote the record in the studio, where Transmutations, released in March, had reworked their live sets. “Pale Blue Dot” opens the album’s second side, a slow-burn that runs close to five minutes. BALTHVS cut MANIFEST on the rigs they use on stage, running analogue direct systems from Chile’s DSM Humboldt alongside their Fender instruments, with Bogotá producer Christian Cifuentes at the board. Across the record the trio push their psychedelic funk towards drum and bass, a harder rock attack and Ethio-jazz. items.body: For the second episode of our Musical Road to WOMEX, we go from Caracas to Berlin by way of a conservatory in Barquisimeto, the route that shaped Gotopo into one of the more unclassifiable voices on the Afro-Latin Dance circuit. She runs Afro-Indigenous Venezuelan rhythm through techno production until neither side gives way, calls the result Ancestral Futurism, and stages it with a female-warrior aesthetic built as much for main-room dancefloors as festival fields. She started at the conservatory in Barquisimeto and came up through El Sistema, the youth-orchestra system that’s put instruments in the hands of generations of Venezuelan kids. She left for Berlin afterward and started over, busking to get by while she learned German. Her stage name comes from her own family history: Gotopo was the last indigenous chief of the region her family comes from. Nobody in her family had kept that history. She found it herself, digging through records nobody else had bothered to look at. She’s described the discovery as grief and celebration arriving together, something erased and something recovered in the same breath. Her 2023 debut EP, Sacúdete, followed, released on Waxploitation, the label built around Gnarls Barkley and Danger Mouse, with Don Elektron and Bomba Estéreo’s Simón Mejía among the collaborators. The reach has widened fast since. The title track ended up soundtracking Major League Soccer’s entire 2024 season, and a newer single, “Mi Gente Lo Siente,” is currently running under the trailer for Valorant Masters 2026. This October she brings that sound to Las Palmas de Gran Canaria at WOMEX’s Club Summit, the strand built around club and electronic sound from across the world. You trained in the conservatory and El Sistema, then found your own voice in Europe by reaching back to your Afro-Indigenous roots. What was the turning point that set that direction? When you take distance you start seeing things you never noticed before or comprehend them much deeper and from new points of view. The music conservatory planted in me a seed of discomfort of existing inside a music education that was so Eurocentric. Then ironically enough, it was Europe that gave me the space to explore how an ancestor of the future could exist in 202+. WOMEX lands this year in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, an Atlantic island whose timple itself carries old Latin American trade routes back across the ocean. As a Venezuelan artist, what are you most curious to discover about that shared history there? Because of the mass migration of Venezuelans I learnt that there’s a huge Canarian community in Venezuela spanning a few decades, people who saw in Venezuela a place to thrive, which it was, and now of course, it’s a reversed migration of kids and grand-kids back to Canaria… I’m obsessed with history and this one promises to be a huge adventure: What dishes will I taste here that will remind me of home? Or maybe slang words that were Venezuelan and landed here, or the opposite? It’s sooo weird in a cool way, I’m so curious! Your work fuses ritual and rave, the sacred and the synthetic. In a WOMEX programme full of traditions, what makes that fusion distinctly yours, and what do you want people to take from your showcase? Groove and vocals are the 2 cores of the most ancient musical memories we hold as humans… sometimes I think that we sang before we even spoke. I always want to make sure that my music makes you move, to me there is nothing more ancestral than groove, and in a Gotopo show you will hardly leave without having collectively sang along with a bunch of strangers WOMEX always sparks unexpected meetings. Which artists, labels or collaborators are you hoping to cross paths with in Las Palmas? There are festivals that I love because of their eclecticism and how they don’t care about Genre but rather about energy. THIS! This is so important for music, for culture and for human connection! I know the festival scene is going through challenging times for several reasons, specially the way kids discover and connect with music is changing… so I don’t blame festivals having to make tough decisions, and including upcoming acts in that equation is a challenge. But I also hope to see a future of festival/event curation where instead of falling for the extremes of either “play safe and book what the listener wants” or “I just book what I like”, promoters and bookers truly put an effort into understanding TikTok and new audiences and how these two are reprogramming people’s way to connect with culture. If you understand something you can hack it for your purpose, kinda, you know? It would be so sad if the curator’s experience of music and culture became isolated from the new generations. I do my job as an artist on social media, but curators, bookers and promoters who also understand this and actively work to stay up-to-date are definitely people I want to meet. Your live shows are as much performance and ritual as concert. How does a room of delegates change how you bring that energy? That’s a great question… I don’t think I want to change absolutely anything about my show. Gran Canaria sits at a mid-Atlantic crossroads between Africa, Europe and the Americas — exactly the between-worlds space you describe as a Latina in Germany. Does a place like that speak to your work? So much! And it makes me interested at a human level before anything, it’s an area I have yet to explore and it’s so exciting to perform in a place where there are so many ancient traces of you… of our constant migrations and cultural exchanges as humans which remind one another: this is what makes us pretty awesome as a humanity. If you could write a personal invitation to the people of Las Palmas to come and discover your showcase, what would it say? Have you heard about this girl from Venezuela? Some of her songs are catchy like Shakira but she’s a bit weirder.   Gotopo plays WOMEX 26's Club Summit in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria 21–25 October, at the Auditorio Alfredo Kraus   PLAYLIST: GOTOPO X RHYTHM PASSPORT   You can find all the previous episodes of Musical Road to Womex HERE   The post Musical Road to WOMEX 2026 – Gotopo appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: I've said it before and I will say it again: it takes a lot to get me interested in "classic" post-rock these days. I won't rehash my complaints here but suffice it to say that I think that thirty odd years of build ups and crescendos is more than enough. And yet, there are still bands operating within the space who have, for lack of a better word, "the juice". Even if the track structures are not exactly revolutionary, the passion and drive of the group makes the good ol' formula beat with invigorated force. Winter At Sea is a phenomenal example. Made up of members from other blog-favored groups (like Flies Are Spies From Hell and Din Of Celestial Birds), their music is steeped with a sense of melancholic loss and dogged hope that I find hard to resist. Head on down to listen to Hearts below to see what I mean. Hearts by Winter At Sea Oh boy. Hearts is a one track, twenty minutes journey into the depths of a murky ocean or rather the decrepit structures that still eke out a life at its shore. The classic post-rock components are all there - the tremolo picked, delay-heavy guitars, the ponderous drums, the sonorous bass. Everything is likewise arranged into the classic post-rock structure, the slow build up and eventual catharsis of the five pieces contained within this one track/album. But something just clicks, you know? Like I said above, there is a passion here, a drive. It's not just familiar notes on a page or mechanical instructions being carried out. It's a performance.As always, I can't really tell you why this works where other music like it doesn't. But I can show it you by playing the music itself. That's part of the beauty and challenge of music, right? It is unmediated. It speaks to us directly. Or not. This kind of post-rock, for me, these days, either speaks to me in this fashion or not at all. And Winter At Sea do, piercing me to the core with their deft approach to sorrow, memory, persistence, and hard-won triumph.

items.body: 発行：白水社 発行日：2026/03/30 発行元ウェブサイト：https://www.hakusuisha.co.jp/book/b673712.html 白水Uブックスの新シリーズ「思想の地平線」の一冊として刊行された本書は、アンリ・ベルクソンによる1889年の著書の翻訳である。本書はベルクソンのいわゆる「四大主著」の第一のものとして知られ、一般に『時間と自由』というタイトルで世に知られてきた（フランス語の原題は『意識に直接与えられたものについての試論』だが、ポグソンによる英訳書以来、しばしばこの通称によって流通している）。なお、本訳書はフランス文学者の平井啓之（1921-1992）が1965年に「ベルグソン全集」の一巻として発表したものを親本としており、1990年の「イデー選書」に続き二度目の再版となる。 哲学書としての本書の魅力は、われわれが「感覚」や「感情」に対して抱く先入見を根本から払拭してくれることにある。例えば、わたしたちはよく喜びや痛みを比較可能なものとして扱う──「タンスに足の小指をぶつける」よりも「ドアに手の指を挟まれる」ほうが痛い、というふうに。しかし、この二つの痛みはほんとうに比較可能なのだろか。この二つの痛みは、本来それぞれに固有な「質」をもっているのであって、それを「どちらが痛いか」という「量」の問題に変換するとき、それぞれのもつ「質」は決定的に取り逃がされてしまうのではないだろうか。これは怒りや悲しみといった感情について考えてみるとき、よりいっそう納得できるものとなるだろう（日常的なやりとりにおいて、人は比較不可能な「怒り」や「悲しみ」をしばしば比較可能なものとして扱うが、それは端的に誤謬である）。本書が全篇にわたって問題とするのは、この「質」と「量」、さらには「時間」と「空間」の混同をはじめとするさまざまな取り違えである。 本書の（英語版の）表題が言わんとすることを端的に整理するなら、おおよそ次のようになるだろう。つまり、わたしたちが経験する（本当の意味での）時間を、その空間的な表象と混同してはならない。ベルクソンが「持続（durée）」と呼ぶところの真の時間を、空間的な語彙によって言い表わすことはできない。自由は、さながらゲームの選択肢のようにX or Y or Zという選択肢のなかから選び取られるものではなく、わたしたちの内的な自我から発する行為の連続のうちにある（X or Y or Zという選択肢は、いわばその「ありえた選択肢」を事後的に表象したものにすぎない）。わたしたちの自由は、持続という流れつつある時間のなかで実現される。人間に自由などないとする決定論も、それに反対する非決定論も、この単純な事実を取り逃がしている。本書の序文において、ベルクソンは「持続と延長」「継起と同時性」「質と量」等々の混同さえ一掃できれば、自由の存在に対する異論も、あるいは自由の問題そのものも、きれいに解消されると述べている（12頁）。そのうえでベルクソンは、決定論者と非決定論者の双方が拠って立つ前提を掘り崩しつつ、われわれの内奥にある深い自我の表現あるいは行為を「自由」と呼ぶことを提案するのである。 そんなふうに本書の内容の一端を要約してみたが、このような説明を繰り返すまでもなく、本書は古典的な哲学書の一冊として本邦でも広く読まれてきた。とりわけ今世紀に入ってからは、中村文郎（岩波文庫）、合田正人＋平井靖史（ちくま学芸文庫）、竹内信夫（白水社）による三種類の翻訳が刊行されており、ここ20年ほどは日本語でも目をみはるような研究成果が続々と現われている。そのような状況のなか、ここであえて本書を取り上げるのは、平井啓之が1965年に上梓した本訳書の歴史的意義を考えたいからである。 本書には三浦信孝による解説「平井啓之先生の思い出」が収められているが、そこでは本書の訳者である平井を中心とする、戦後日本の知的状況の一幕が鮮やかに描き出されている。1990年の「イデー選書」に洒脱な解説を寄せた加藤典洋（1948-2019）しかり、平井の遺志を継いでベルクソンの個人全訳（未完）に取り組んだ竹内信夫（1945-2026）しかり、三浦も含めて戦後の一時期には「平井スクール」とでも呼びうるゆるやかな共同体が存在した。そして、表むきはサルトルやランボーを専門とするこのフランス文学者が「その全集にほぼ目を通したと言い得る唯一の思想家」（264頁）こそベルクソンであり、そうした思い入れあってこそ、あるところでは小林秀雄のベルクソン論に対して徹底的な批判を加えもしたのである（「小林秀雄の「ベルグソン論」について」［1987］）。 以上を約言すれば、いまから半世紀以上前に世に出た本訳書の周囲には、戦後日本の思想・文学・批評を貫通する知られざる鉱脈が広がっているということだ。古典の新訳や解説ばかりが重宝される風潮のなかにあって、こうした先達の訳業がふたたび人目にふれる機会を得られたことを、心から喜ばしく思う。 執筆日：2026/07/31（金）

items.album: 松房子｜「黒坂圭太──森を見ずに木を見る」

items.excerpt: 会期：2026/06/15～2026/07/18 会場：武蔵野美術大学 美術館・図書館［東京都］ 公式サイト：https://mauml.musabi.ac.jp/museum/events/23064/ 武蔵野美術大学美術館で、アニメーション作家・黒坂圭太の展覧会「黒坂圭太──森を見ずに木を見る」が開催された。本展は黒坂が長年にわたり教鞭を執ってきた同大映像学科の教授退任を記念する企画展である。 黒坂は武蔵野美大の油絵学科を卒業したのち、イメージフォーラム映像研究所や京都芸術短期大学に通い、16mmフィルムを用いた実験映像の制作を始める。映像学科には1990年の設立から携わり、昨年度末に定年を迎えて30年を超える教員生活に区切りをつけた★1。展覧会ではアニメーション作品の上映やそれらの資料群に加えて、10代の頃に描いていた油画から最新作の大型ドローイングまでが紹介され、彼の創作人生の軌跡をたどる構成となっていた。 「森を見ずに木を見る」展［筆者撮影］ 黒坂の資料を見ていて驚かされるのは、アニメーションの制作過程で生まれる中間生成物の緻密さである。鉛筆で描かれる原画の筆致はもちろん、フ
items.body: 会期：2026/06/15～2026/07/18 会場：武蔵野美術大学 美術館・図書館［東京都］ 公式サイト：https://mauml.musabi.ac.jp/museum/events/23064/ 武蔵野美術大学美術館で、アニメーション作家・黒坂圭太の展覧会「黒坂圭太──森を見ずに木を見る」が開催された。本展は黒坂が長年にわたり教鞭を執ってきた同大映像学科の教授退任を記念する企画展である。 黒坂は武蔵野美大の油絵学科を卒業したのち、イメージフォーラム映像研究所や京都芸術短期大学に通い、16mmフィルムを用いた実験映像の制作を始める。映像学科には1990年の設立から携わり、昨年度末に定年を迎えて30年を超える教員生活に区切りをつけた★1。展覧会ではアニメーション作品の上映やそれらの資料群に加えて、10代の頃に描いていた油画から最新作の大型ドローイングまでが紹介され、彼の創作人生の軌跡をたどる構成となっていた。 「森を見ずに木を見る」展［筆者撮影］ 黒坂の資料を見ていて驚かされるのは、アニメーションの制作過程で生まれる中間生成物の緻密さである。鉛筆で描かれる原画の筆致はもちろん、フィルムコンテやグラフィックスコアと呼ばれる視覚的な設計図にも目を見張る。 「森を見ずに木を見る」展［筆者撮影］ 展覧会の入り口には黒坂の直筆で「私はこれまで木だけを見てきました。おそらくこの先も森を見ることはできないでしょう。」と掲げられている。また第1章のパネルには「描くことではなく、祖父自身の『ドラマ』を描き出すことが好きだった」という発言も記され、自らの関心事に対する局所的な視点と、人生の来し方を視覚化することへの興味が明かされている。 2011年の震災以降、黒坂は線がうごめくようなドローイングアニメーションを制作してきた。それらは線や風景を主体とする出来事の変遷、すなわち「ドラマ」を表現したものだといえる。この手法による代表作《山川景子は振り向かない》は、変わり続ける風景という対象を山、川、景、子なる名のもとに擬人化し、その行く末を鉛筆による線とデジタル編集におけるディゾルブによって表現している。そこでは「山川景子」というキャラクターが人間の似姿を取ったり、「木」や「水」といった具体的な対象が躍動したりするような表現は志向されない。彼の作品にアニミスム的な生命感が見出されるとすれば、それは描かれた表象ではなく、線そのものにおいてである。 「森を見ずに木を見る」展［筆者撮影］ 本展ではマンガ作品《ママのハンカチ》の原画や、新作アニメーション《たらちね（仮）》の試作パートも観ることができた。《たらちね（仮）》は彼が「画劇」と呼ぶライブドローイングに基づくもので、長年におよぶ創作活動の集大成的な作品になることが期待される。ただただ、その完成が待ち遠しい。 鑑賞日：2026/07/10（金） ★1──金沢美術工芸大学大学院映像コースでは、現在も客員教授に名を連ねている。 URL=https://www.kanazawa-bidai.ac.jp/faculty/research1/movie/

items.body: The stars appear first. Their light seems to have traveled through the interior of a violin before reaching us, gathering the grain of wood and the pressure of a human hand along the way. Throughout Maksimal, Daniel Temkin thus treats music as celestial mapmaking, drawing places where the horizon turns out to be an instrument played from both sides. The title composition, written in 2022, carries the genetic traces of the Baroque concerto grosso into a world of fractured memory and unstable terrain. Francisco Fullana is the violin soloist, giving the music its incandescent center. Ryan McAdams conducts the Maksimal Ensemble with a keen understanding of the score’s shifting scale, allowing its smallest gestures to retain their mystery even as the orchestral field opens around them. “White Heat” begins with bells and glockenspiel drawing an aperture through which the violin’s restless language can spill across the page of the sky. Images arrive with a precision unavailable to the crude constellations of ordinary imagination, bearing the spirit of something immeasurable yet intimately knowable. Temkin’s orchestration blooms in radiant layers, creating enough space for the violin to run and fly without severing its connection to the ensemble. Fullana’s virtuosity serves as a vehicle for the music’s spirited intelligence, while winds and percussion orbit his line, occasionally catching its light. “Continuum” begins with the violin alone, carving space from time with resolute purpose while scarcely disturbing the air around it. As the orchestra unfolds along the periphery, molecular connections form between vanished cities and the people who once carried those urban spaces inside them. The piano exhales, while the brass catches and draws that breath underground. Though relatively brief, the movement produces the peculiar sensation of arrival. “Circle Games” then opens in buoyant motion before pivoting into contemplation, tracing a recurring exchange between outward momentum and inward gravity. The music brushes against the open-spaced pastoralism one might associate with Copland, yet its landscape keeps slipping beyond the trappings of such comparisons. Dreamed Landscapes, composed between 2017 and 2018 and rendered joyfully by pianist Ryan MacEvoy McCullough, brings this cartographic impulse into a more private cosmos. “Starfield” welcomes us into light as darkness’s fullest utterance, an illumination generated from within the black fabric itself. Dance-inflected steps puncture that fabric and reveal flashes of an alien expressivity, briefly exposing a grammar whose syntax exceeds the human nervous system. The suspicion of otherness soon becomes one that consciousness has always been plural. In “Glaciers crumbling, assembling,” the title’s entropy enters immediately through blocky textures and splintering masses. Fragments break loose from an immense harmonic body, while reformation becomes audible only in the ensuing silence, in which absence begins arranging the wreckage into a structure the ear can enter but never see. “Echoes of the Horizon” draws the cycle’s luminous points into its large-scale dissolutions. The insistent left hand establishes the fundament, while the right hand opens the firmament, hurling packets of emotional voltage across the distance between them. Under McCullough’s touch, the piano becomes a machine for folding vastness until mountains and oceans briefly occupy the same trembling surface. Ocean’s Call, composed in 2015 and revised in 2021, is a string quartet inspired by Big Sur and its environs. The Aizuri Quartet performs it with grace and exacting acuity, preserving the music’s sensuousness without softening its strange geological awareness. In “Hanging Cliffs, Rising Mist,” the cello draws a taut rope of purpose through the texture as the higher strings make room for a rising sun. Pizzicato details become lunar phases, while gradual coalescences deepen the field and pull the listener toward “The Bitter Salt of the Sea.” This central movement speaks in whispers, each phrase carrying the friction between water and air. The strummed cello sends tremors toward the crests of the waves, and the developing urgency becomes a form of surrender with a pulse still beating inside it. Temkin understands that yielding can possess enormous force and allows the music to lean into that paradox until submission and propulsion become indistinguishable. “Lullaby Waves” carries traces of Chinese folksong into harmonizations of light, setting them aboard a vessel woven from tenderness. As it travels farther across the water, the vessel gradually sheds the jurisdiction of the visible world. Across this recording, Temkin teaches the ear to draw maps, then quietly removes the territory beneath the pencil. Memory emerges as the architect of dimensions in which the vanished can continue to resonate. The sky finally collapses into the dark anatomy of listening itself, pierced by the patient apertures we once mistook for stars. The post Daniel Temkin: Maksimal appeared first on Sequenza21.

items.body: KKKAAARRREEENNNIIINNNAAA captures a 2025 performance that the three artists did together in London Charlemagne Palestine, Oren Ambarchi and Daniel O'Sullivan are releasing a collaborative album, titled KKKAAARRREEENNNIIINNNAAA. Consisting of one extended piece, the record captures a May 2025 live performance that the three artists did together at London's Cafe OTO. The set saw the trio reimagine a key vocal work of Palestine's, Karenina, which he originally recorded in Paris in March 1997. In this version, O'Sullivan controls three cassette machines playing the original recording, and also plays viola, synths and adds live vocals. Ambarchi contributes guitar, while Palestine adds his live voice and plays keyboard. Black Truffle will release KKKAAARRREEENNNIIINNNAAA on 11 September 2026. ... items.album: HIROMI UEHARA Hiromi's Sonicbloom: Time Control (Jazz Rock/Fusion, 2007)
items.excerpt: Review by Fercandio46 — There is something distinctive that makes Hiromi a jazz pianist whose albums transcend the genre; she grew up listening to 70s fusion and progressive bands, incorporating those harmonies into her music. Consequently, with her group Sonicbloom, those "spacey" explorations and ethereal sounds became more prominent, heightened by the presence of David Fiuczynski, an exquisite avant-garde guitarist whose style defies simple categorization, though it undoubtedly reflects
items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — There is something distinctive that makes Hiromi a jazz pianist whose albums transcend the genre; she grew up listening to 70s fusion and progressive bands, incorporating those harmonies into her music. Consequently, with her group Sonicbloom, those "spacey" explorations and ethereal sounds became more prominent, heightened by the presence of David Fiuczynski, an exquisite avant-garde guitarist whose style defies simple categorization, though it undoubtedly reflects the legacy of Allan Holdsworth. With this group, she created a concept album for her debut centered on the theme of time, as evidenced by the titles of the tracks."Time Difference" possesses both classical sensibility and the surgical, energetic precision of King Crimson. It engages the piano in a dialogue with the drums and guitar, then shifts to keyboard work accompanied by the electric bass."Time Out" features a funkier, more urban and cosmopolitan Groove, evoking a nighttime cocktail hour amidst marquee lights, the din of the crowd, and the sounds of traffic, while the guitar plays dissonant scales and the piano and bass cut through the air with tightly interlocking notes. The band becomes the soundtrack to a New York party, and the balance between experimentation and pure listening pleasure reaches its peak.A tranquil atmosphere with an Oriental feel, as if the spirit of Ryuichi Sakamoto had drifted in through the window, permeates Time Travel; naturally, the influence of Chick Corea's groups, such as Return to Forever and the Elektric Band, is also present. Hiromi is a fine exponent of "progressive jazz," though a different kind than that found in bands like Graham Parker's Strata or Red Kite. David Fiuczynski can play jazz, funk, or the more daring styles heard in Screaming Headless Torsos (another of his bands), while Hiromi continues to play and experiment with sounds alongside the band; at times they sound like a 1970s jam session, shifting to an 80s vibe, and finally landing on 90s fusi�n, a fitting progression, given that the album revolves around the concept of time."Deep Into the Night" reveals another, purely jazz-oriented dimension; it also offers a perfect opportunity to recommend her album with Stanley Clarke, where her piano prowess transcends mere virtuosity to convey ideas and emotions, capturing the spirit of classic jazz that she revives, offering the best of both worlds.A concept difficult to define, that chasm between what one feels and the divide between internal and external reality, is explored in "Real Clock vs. Body Clock = Jet Lag," a track where the meter is as complex as the message itself. Fiuczynski's guitar sounds as if it were melting in the midst of a surrealist act, yet at times she plays as if she were back in the 1920s. "Time and Space" is another gem (the entire album is, truth be told) and reminded me of another master well worth recommending: Misha Mengelberg and his album "Who's Bridge". In that trio setting with Daryl Jones and Joey Baron, they play with time and surprises much like Sonicbloom does here.Classical music takes time by surprise, and a fugue kicks off "Time Control" (or "Controlled by Time"), naturally bringing to mind Keith Emerson, who inhabited that same intersection of classical and jazz, before the band pulls us into the present; the Rhodes piano climbs powerfully alongside the group, reaching the very peaks of the genre and transcending them, with Fiuczynski playing his fretless guitar.Time Flies offers another moment to catch one's breath, a space where a sigh rises toward the sky, mingling with rooftops and treetops, for this album encompasses both day and night! Adventure transforms into fun and reflection; concept albums can be a delightful experience, culminating in an epic finale and the track "Time's Up" (which features a bonus track on the Japanese edition). Here, the band flows like a river, leaving genres behind on the Banks, held back by the stones, until only the purest, most transparent music remains.

items.excerpt: Review by Steve Conrad — Well, They LOOK "Normal"!Rick Whitehurst, I mean. Who, along with Krystal Pavlovic, have composed and performed "Spider", under the 'current' name of BAKULLAMA & KRYSTAL.I say 'current', since as you can plainly see, if you actually do look at the fine- and not so fine- print, that there is also the "EX BAKU LLAMA" moniker, as well as (if you query BAKULLAMA on ProgArchives, you will ALSO see BAKU), and yes, now "BAKULLAMA & KRYSTAL".So maybe even the esteemed Prog
items.body: Review by Steve Conrad — Well, They LOOK "Normal"!Rick Whitehurst, I mean. Who, along with Krystal Pavlovic, have composed and performed "Spider", under the 'current' name of BAKULLAMA & KRYSTAL.I say 'current', since as you can plainly see, if you actually do look at the fine- and not so fine- print, that there is also the "EX BAKU LLAMA" moniker, as well as (if you query BAKULLAMA on ProgArchives, you will ALSO see BAKU), and yes, now "BAKULLAMA & KRYSTAL".So maybe even the esteemed ProgArchives is confused.BAKULLAMA et alNear as I can piece it together- and I'm probably making way more of this than I need to, such is the burden of almost achieving OCD status- multitalented Rick has been at the heart of the BAKULLAMA enterprise since 2007, falling off the map (well, really, landing in Washington, resurrecting the music-making, with an impressive assortment of singles and albums in his/their discography.Of which, "Spider" is the latest release. And I found it meekly and humbly waiting to be reviewed, right here on the venerable ProgArchives.Patiently, seems to me.SpiderHere's (at least on Bandcamp) a nine track album.I say THIS, since you will notice (again, if you choose to peruse) the track list here on this site is only SEVEN tracks, almost all of them different versions than are to be found on Bandcamp, what can I say.And, to further complicate matters, even if on Bandcamp we can actually hear (I assume Krystal) singing in a husky and slightly world-weary manner, the only track that lists "lyrics", actually gives us the information: "none".The tracks that DO have lyrics, don't provide them.QuirkYes, the impression I need to impart is that although these two fine musicians APPEAR to be "normal" (and I'm willing to entertain as legitimate the observation you may choose to make, "What is normal"?), the music is rather a different tale to tell.For instance, in the ProgArchives forum inviting hapless reviewers to please take note of patiently waiting albums, someone (I just don't think it was Valdez, but who really knows), makes this statement: "It's a pop/electronic/prog hybrid of an album."Personally, I suspect Rick is behind this description, but I've been wrong before.I Couldn't ResistNo, this album is certainly eclectic, and certainly has electronica tones. There are some actual instruments, at least a Fender acoustic guitar and an Epiphone SG bass guitar are listed, and as far as I can tell, Krystal actually does use her actual vocal chords.These two pranksters eschew conventional forms and patterns, choosing instead to tempt and taunt the listener with sometimes spooky, odd, off-center, and just plain goofy fun while making music together.The liner notes say this seductively unusual commentary about "Spider": "A different and moody ode to Spiders, Birds, Mermaids... and Dreams."It's Just Cool, OKI like this. I think of "progressive", and it might at times mean "pushing boundaries", correct? It might mean breaking some rules and using off-beat humor and maybe sometimes, just not paying much attention to convention.Check. Check. Check.Anyhow, I'll not say more.C'mon. Take a chance! Who knows- a collection of nine, or six, or howEVER many tuneful explorations of zaniness MIGHT be just the ticket on such a day as this.My rating: 3.25 sarcastic stanzas out of a possible 5- good. And Slightly more than non-essential.

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — These Arizona bros are definitely hooked on Krautrock ala Neu!, Can, Tangerine Dream and more of thekind. Soundscapes of Tangerine Dream, Cluster, early-Kraftwerk and the hypnotic "motorik" rock ofNeu! or Can. However, Trees Speak take 1970s German experimental rock & electronic music and puttheir own modern spin on them. Too bad they don't expand (read extend) more some of those greatideas (some of these tracks are way too short, IMHO), thus inducing a bit of a frustration in termsof depth - though this is never shallow, au contraire. One can only wonder if they'd dared plunginginto epic-length sonic explorations that Froese & Co. had done in their heydays.We've got a series of 16 short soundscapes (none over 4-mins) that are +/- fused into each other,and they transport you into the realms of synth and computer servers and other electronicsnightmares, and it's rather addictive, partly because there are real drums and a few more realinstruments played by guests (some will return on the next albums). The middle of the album , fromSadness of Wires until the title track is one amazing trip in copper and silicium. AFAIAC, my favetrack is Chamber Of Frequencies, where 'trons and and guitars create a special little plus.Though the following albums are of the same ilk, I must that none of them have resonated as muchwith my eardrums as their debut Ohms, partly because the surprise is gone. Impossible to pull outthe CD for only one sole listen: minimum two or three plays and it usually remains close to the deckfor possible more spins before heading (finally) back into the shelf. My 3.5 stars are of course notobjective, because Post-Human probably deserve as much as their previous releases, but I can't helpbeing subjective, not having that "Wow" factor.

items.body: Review by ProgExpert — It is amazing to hear H�llas go fully prog on *Panorama*. The record feels broader, more ambitious, and more mature than ever, while still retaining the melodic instinct and personality that make the band distinctive. I only wish a few especially beautiful musical ideas had been explored further, particularly the passage around 3:30 in the first suite and the wonderful final theme at the very end of the last song. Those moments are so strong that I wanted them to keep unfolding. It is brilliant to hear these artists growing in ambition and maturity. We simply cannot have enough of this music.

items.body: Review by ProgExpert — This is a remarkably delicate and sensitive record, played with exceptional taste throughout. Every arrangement feels carefully judged... nothing is overstated, and the musicianship is consistently impressive without ever becoming showy. There is a warmth and naturalness to the playing that gives the music an almost timeless quality! At several moments, it recalls the more pastoral and adventurous side of 1970s Caravan, with that same combination of melodic richness, subtle complexity, and effortless flow. What stands out most, though, is the restraint. Beautifully performed, elegant, and deeply musical. I cannot get enough, I wish they had composed 10 records! Not just 2! Come back Jouis!

items.body: Review by ValeriyK — Karfagen ? OMNI II Act I: The Glass of TimeOMNI II Act I: The Glass of Time continues the story started with OMNI, released by Antony Kalugin in 2025. And, without any doubt, OMNI II is one of the brightest progressive rock releases of 2026.A wonderful cast of musicians, clear and rich production and, most importantly, strong melodies make OMNI II a very enjoyable album from beginning to end. There is a lot of good music here, and I have already returned to this album many times.Like the previous OMNI, the music is divided into larger chapters. Here we have OMNI Part 4, Part 5 and the bonus Part 6, each approximately the length of one vinyl side.OMNI Part 4The album opens with The Glass of Time Part 1, and what a pleasure it is to hear Rob Reed here. For almost the first minute and forty seconds, it is basically Rob's world: keyboards, guitars and bass. Then Michel St-P�re and Antony Kalugin join in and the piece develops into a wonderful instrumental with a strong classic Genesis and Tony Banks flavour. It is a beautiful and very natural opening to the album.The second track, Frozen Rivers, is without doubt one of the highlights of the album. Here we meet the wizard Roine Stolt, one of the finest composers and guitarists in modern progressive rock, together with his brother Michael Stolt on bass. There is a very strong Scandinavian feeling running through this composition. Kalugin has mentioned that he wrote this song especially for Roine, and even the lyrics seem to reflect that connection.It is also a pleasure to hear John Hackett again on flute and Marek Arnold on soprano saxophone. Everything comes together beautifully, and the lyrics have a warm and soulful quality. For me, this is one of those tracks that immediately makes you want to press repeat.Then comes Shadowbound, and this is simply a hit. In another musical universe I could easily imagine this song appearing at Eurovision and doing very well there. It has an immediate melody and a memorable chorus, but underneath that accessible surface there is still plenty happening.The song deals with destiny, our choices and the struggle between different sides of ourselves. Mariya Panasenko is the real star here. Her performance is powerful, emotional and technically excellent, while Jannica Lund adds beautiful backing vocals and Roine Stolt contributes guitar. In the middle the song suddenly opens into a symphonic art-rock section. Somehow Karfagen manages to put Eurovision and progressive rock into the same four minutes ? and it works!Part 4 closes with The Shape of Love, featuring Marco Gl�hmann of Sylvan. Marco is surely one of the most distinctive vocalists in contemporary progressive rock. His voice is immediately recognisable, and the emotional range he brings to a song is remarkable.Just as The Last Card was one of my favourite moments on the first OMNI, The Shape of Love is one of the strongest songs here. It is also nice to hear Kalugin writing so openly about love again. I sincerely hope Marco will return for the next chapter of OMNI, because his voice brings so much emotion to this music.OMNI Part 5Part 5 begins with the nine-minute Carry On, and my only complaint is that I wish it were even longer!This is warm, vintage progressive rock, somewhere in the world of Alan Parsons and Electric Light Orchestra, but still unmistakably Karfagen. Yogi Lang of RPWL provides his characteristic vocals, and the composition develops through two rather different moods. The first section is energetic, positive, almost feel-good prog, while the second becomes more balladic and has, to my ears, something of the spirit of classic ELO.Kalle Wallner, also well known from RPWL and Blind Ego, appears on guitar, and it is great to see these two Bavarian musicians together on a Karfagen album. Michael Stolt once again provides his strong and dependable bass work.Beyond the Mirror brings back Per Malmberg, whom listeners of the first OMNI may remember from The Spark. Pascal Gutman adds Chapman Stick, and the result is another melodic and very positive song.And finally we hear Antony himself singing a verse! One thing I noticed on this album is that there is actually not very much lead vocal from Kalugin. Of course this is his artistic decision, but personally I enjoy his voice and hope to hear more of it on future albums.There is also a lovely moment in the middle of Beyond the Mirror where Jannica Lund's backing vocals meet acoustic guitar. Believe it or not, it reminds me of Fleetwood Mac ? that old, warm, soft pop-rock feeling ? and it fits surprisingly well.How Fragile We Are is a charming, enveloping and very gentle ballad. Mariya Panasenko sings beautifully, while Marek Arnold's soprano saxophone almost answers her voice like a second singer in a duet. Antony can also be heard on backing vocals in the chorus.There is something very Gilmour-like and Pink Floyd-like about the atmosphere here. Nothing is rushed. The song simply breathes, until we are left with the words: "Oh, how fragile we are?"The main album then closes with The Glass of Time Part 2, bringing us back to Rob Reed. Once again, for roughly the opening minute and forty seconds, Rob carries almost everything himself ? keyboards, guitar and bass. :)It works like a mirror of The Glass of Time Part 1, bringing the main album full circle. This is Karfagen instrumental music in its natural territory, with another gentle touch of Genesis and Tony Banks. A wonderful ending to the main 48-minute album.But fortunately, the CD does not stop there.OMNI Part 6 ? The Silent CompassInstead of releasing another separate Working Tapes disc this time, Kalugin has included the complete OMNI Part 6, lasting just over nineteen minutes, as a bonus chapter on the CD. This material has also been announced as a separate digital release titled The Silent Compass, coming to streaming platforms this Friday. But CD listeners receive the whole additional chapter together with the main album. Thank you, Antony!It begins with Under the Northern Lights, a tiny piece lasting less than two minutes, but what a beautiful two minutes they are. This is almost classical music: piano, organ and orchestral colours, soprano saxophone, Roine Stolt's guitar and John Hackett's flute. There is something of Edvard Grieg in its atmosphere, perfectly matching the northern mood suggested by the title. A miniature symphonic pleasure.Then we arrive at The Silent Compass, one of the finest instrumentals on the whole release. Roine Stolt and Roberto D�az of Anima Mundi create a wonderful dialogue between their guitars. Max Velychko provides excellent acoustic guitar and John Hackett opens the piece beautifully on flute.There are shades of Anthony Phillips and The Flower Kings here, but ultimately this is Karfagen doing what Karfagen does best: melodic, pastoral and symphonic progressive rock with plenty of space for the musicians to tell their own stories.OM
